newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Jordan says price stability debate wide open.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Jordan says price stability debate wide open.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Jerry Jordan on Thursday said the debate about price stability and the timeframe needed to achieve that Fed objective remains wide open.

"I can't answer that because the only way to be answered is to talk in terms of what you mean by price stability, how you know you can be there, how you are going to measure it," Jordan told Reuters in response to a question about the timeframe the Fed is looking to achieve its most often-stated goal.
Jordan, who spoke at the Ohio Bankers Day conference, said the notion of price stability itself as a desirable policy goal is not shared by everyone.

"I hear a lot of people telling me that they think it's wrong to have price stability (as the central bank's objective)," Jordan said. "I hear people, including bankers, saying 'What's wrong with inflation?' I hear Congressmen saying that."
Jordan noted an important issue is the measure of price stability because "opinions are all over the lot. It's a question of distribution. It's like forecasts."
He added that price stability may differ by region or demographic group because of the difference in price behavior in various segments of the economy.
"Prices are going down on computers, compact discs, refrigerators. And other people are saying 'the price of things I buy is going up'," Jordan said.

Jordan said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan best approached the price performance issue by saying the Fed will have achieved its goal when inflation is no longer a concern in household or business decisions.

"We are trying to create the conditions where people make their decisions about the future in the expectation that the purchasing power of the currency will be about the same as it is now," Jordan said.

He also noted that price stability is only one issue in the Fed's "basic mission ... to maximize standards of living over time by ensuring stable financial conditions, (a stable) payments system and a stable economy."

Jordan also took a stab at Wall Street economists who put much stock in the theory of the non-accelerating inflationary rate of unemployment (NAIRU) and who try to anticipate Fed policy moves based on the jobless rate.
Wall Street analysts may be the only group still concerned with the notion that low unemployment fuels inflation, Jordan said.
Jordan, like Lee Hoskins, his predecessor at the Cleveland Fed, advocates targeting some measure of inflation to conduct monetary policy.
The notion has gained support within the Fed. New York Fed President William McDonough has proposed targeting the core Consumer Price Index in a 0.5- to 2.0-percent range.
